title: Who will be awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as the recipient of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, expected to be announced by the Norwegian Nobel Committee on October 9, 2026.

If the prize is awarded to an individual not named in the listed options, this question will resolve as **Other individual**. If it is awarded to a non-individual recipient not named in the listed options, it will resolve as **Other organization**.

If no prize is awarded for any reason this question will be **annulled**.
fine_print: If the prize is shared, this question will resolve as the option naming one of the recipients. If more than one recipient is named in the options or if none is, it will resolve according to the recipient listed first in the official announcement by the Norwegian Nobel Committee.

comments.author: Theomachado
comments.text:
## **The most probable outcome is that the winner will be someone not currently listed.**

**Fact 1: The market is not only noisy regarding this event, but it also consistently misprices outcomes.** In 2025, with \$23 million in volume, the eventual winner was priced at only **0.8% two days before the announcement**. The favorite, Navalnaya (9.5%), did not win. The second favorite, Trump (5.7%), also lost. Although Machado was *listed,* the market assigned her a probability forty times lower than the incorrect favorite.

**Fact 2: This pattern is not unique to one year; there is a consistent mechanism.** The committee prioritizes moral clarity with minimal political cost. Prediction market prominence reflects political salience, which often makes a candidate less likely to be chosen. Highly traded figures such as Trump, Zelenskyy, Netanyahu, and Modi are avoided by the committee for this reason. Previous winners like Nihon Hidankyo, ICAN, the Tunisian Quartet, Ressa/Muratov, and Bialiatski were not market favorites. Therefore, m**arket prominence is at best uninformative and may even be a negative indicator.**

**Fact 3: The nominee pool is large, while the list of named candidates is small. There are 287 nominees: 208 individuals and 79 organiz**ations. **Metaculus lists 3 individuals (1.4% of the pool) and 6 organizations (7.6%).** For these named options to represent the majority probability, salience would need to concentrate probability by a **factor of 20 to 40.** Fact 1 demonstrates that this concentration does not occur.

***

**POLYMARKET**

| Metaculus named options          | 9     | 3.1%  | 33.3% | 27.5% | 3.70% / 3.06% |
| -------------------------------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ------------- |
| Polymarket-listed, not Metaculus | 62    | 21.6% | 33.3% | 17.5% | 0.54% / 0.28% |
| On neither list                  | \~216 | 75.3% | 33.4% | 55.0% | 0.15% / 0.25% |

Polymarket splits almost exactly into thirds. Against a uniform prior of 0.35% per nominee, it concentrates **10.6×** on the Metaculus nine and discounts the unlisted to **0.44×**. comments.author: SharpNimbus
comments.text:
Core Structural Mechanics & Historical Baselines
Base Rate Allocation (78/22 Individual vs. Org): Historically, individuals capture \~78% of awards and organizations \~22%. However, organizational selection concentrates heavily during multi-theater global instability, with humanitarian entities representing 35.4% of all institutional laureates.
The Humanitarian Pivot: When global conflicts present high friction points with collapsed supply lines and severe civilian suffering (Sudan, Gaza, Ukraine), the committee historically tilts away from state leaders toward decentralized grassroots responders. This elevates Sudan's ERRs (20%) as the most robust risk-adjusted position against betting markets.
Political Defiance vs. Operational Neutrality: If the committee chooses an ideological stance against Russian state aggression, Yulia Navalnaya (12%) represents the most direct individual symbol following Alexei Navalny's death. Conversely, awarding wartime heads of state (e.g., Zelenskyy at 5%) directly conflicts with the committee's post-WWII reluctance to honor active military leaders.
Key Scenarios & Probability Distribution
Grassroots Humanitarian Resilience (Sudan ERRs — 20.0%):
Decentralized volunteer response networks operating across acute combat zones in Khartoum and Darfur address the committee’s mandate to spotlight neglected humanitarian disasters without endorsing state actors.
Dissident Courage & Human Rights (Yulia Navalnaya — 12.0%):
Provides an uncompromised moral statement against the Kremlin, fitting past templates like Memorial (2022), Dmitry Muratov (2021), and Liu Xiaobo (2010).
Multilateral Legal Order & International Law (ICJ — 5.0% / UNRWA — 10.0%):
Recognizing the ICJ would signal institutional defense of the Geneva Conventions and international legal architecture. UNRWA carries high humanitarian weight but faces significant political pushback that may cause committee hesitation.
Long-Tail Catch-All Protection (24.0% Aggregate):
Because the Norwegian Nobel Committee operates under a 50-year secrecy rule and frequently departs from external shortlists (including PRIO), allocating 14.0% to Other Individual and 10.0% to Other Organization safeguards against unheralded consensus nominees (e.g., indigenous land rights defenders, press freedom advocates, or global health pioneers).
Resolution Mechanics
Joint Awards: In the event of a divided award (e.g., shared between an individual dissident and an organization, or dual human rights groups), exposure is calibrated toward the primary named entity per standard market resolution protocols.
